description: Hey, I’m Atharv Cloud Computing student, i'm interested in space technology, software development and scientific innovation. Working on the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, combining data visualization and sound.
summary:
EarthSonic turns 47 years of real NASA and NOAA satellite records into a multi-channel audio-visual experience. Four climate datasets — surface temperature anomaly (NASA GISTEMP v4), atmospheric CO₂ (Mauna Loa Observatory), ocean heat content (NOAA NCEI), and sea ice extent (NSIDC) — are each mapped to a distinct audio voice using the STRAUSS sonification framework, so listeners can hear how Earth’s climate has shifted from 1979 to 2026.

The project has two interfaces: a 2D JPL-style mission console with a full timeline scrubber, per-channel mixer, and WAV export; and a WebXR VR mode where users scan a QR code, insert their phone into a headset, and explore a full 3D Earth with HRTF spatial audio anchored to each data channel.

All data assets are genuine public records from NASA, NOAA, and NSIDC — no simulated or procedurally generated values. The goal is to make decades of planetary change perceptible without needing a science background.
details:
EarthSonic is a scientific sonification platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Earth Information Jukebox” track. It maps four continuous satellite telemetry streams to synchronized audio and 3D visuals across a 47-year climate record (1979–2026).

What it does:
Each data channel drives a separate audio voice through the STRAUSS Python sonification library — temperature anomaly controls melodic pitch, CO₂ modulates harmonic saturation, ocean heat drives a sub-bass layer, and sea ice produces high-frequency percussive textures. Users can scrub through the full timeline, mix channels independently, and export the result as a WAV file.

The 3D mission console renders a photorealistic Earth globe (NASA Blue Marble, Black Marble night lights, MODIS cloud composite, GEBCO elevation) with real-time shader responses tied to data values. A separate WebXR VR mode lets mobile users pair via QR code and experience the data spatially in a Google Cardboard headset — no app installation required.

Tools used:
Python, Flask, Gunicorn, STRAUSS, NumPy, SciPy, SoundFile — backend and audio synthesis. Three.js (r128) for the 3D mission console. Babylon.js for the WebXR orbital VR mode. Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS — no build system. Tested with 854 pytest assertions and 211 Node.js contract tests.

Why it matters:
Climate data is usually presented as line graphs that require prior context to interpret. Sound bypasses that barrier — pitch and rhythm are perceived instantly, without reading axes or legends. EarthSonic makes multi-decadal change perceptible to anyone, including people with visual impairments.
